title: Where Two Chains Merge
statement:
Two singly linked lists may merge: from some node on, they continue through the very same nodes to the end, like a Y lying on its side. Find the first node they share.

How this version passes nodes. The test runner can only build separate lists, so node identity is stood in for by values: every node has a distinct value, except that the shared tail appears in both lists with the same values in the same order. Treat two nodes with equal values as the same node. Return the value of the first shared node, or -1 if the lists never merge.

Aim for O(m + n) time and O(1) extra memory, and do not change the lists.

examples.why: After 4, 8, 15 and after 42, both lists run through the same nodes 16 → 23.
No node is shared, so both lists end separately.
The lists are the same chain from the very first node.

constraints: Values are distinct except for the shared tail
hints: With extra memory it is easy: remember every node of one list in a set, then walk the other list. Can you do it with two pointers only?
If both lists had the same length before the merge point, two pointers moving in step would meet exactly there. How can you remove the difference in length?
Walk pointer p through A and then B; walk q through B and then A. Both travel the same total distance, so they line up at the merge point, or both reach the end together.

explain.intuition:
Say list A has a nodes before the merge, list B has b, and they share c nodes. If a = b, two pointers stepping together arrive at the merge node at the same moment. The difficulty is only the head start one of them needs.

The trick: when pointer p finishes A, send it to the head of B; when q finishes B, send it to the head of A. Then p walks a + c + b steps before reaching the merge node the second time around, and q walks b + c + a. Same number, so they meet there. If the lists never merge (c = 0), both walk a + b steps and become null at the same time, which ends the loop.
steps: While p and q are not the same node (here: not both null and not equal in value): move each one step; a pointer that falls off its list jumps to the head of the other list.
When the loop stops, p is either the merge node or null.
Return its value, or -1 for null.
pitfalls: Jumping to the other head when the pointer is at the last node instead of when it is null. In lists with no merge, the loop then never ends.
Comparing the lists element by element from the start. The merge point is usually at different positions in the two lists.
Thinking a shared value in the middle means the lists cross and then separate. A node has one next, so once merged they stay merged.

solutions.title: Remember the nodes of one list
solutions.idea: Put every node of A in a set (here: its value). Walk B; the first node found in the set is the merge point.

solutions.title: Cut the head start
solutions.idea: Measure both lengths, advance the longer list's pointer by the difference, then step both together until they meet.

solutions.title: Two pointers that swap lists
solutions.idea: p walks A then B, q walks B then A. Equal total distance makes them meet at the merge node, or at null together.

followups: Why does the swapping version never loop forever when the lists do not merge?
How would you check whether one list has a cycle before looking for a merge point?
